rows.description: A teenager hesitates, raises a brow or says maybe about a plan or belief. Doubt may reflect careful thinking or fear, and open discussion beats pressure.

rows.subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager tries to tell whether a classmate is interested, puzzled or bored from face and voice. These cues are hints only, and asking is better than assuming.

rows.description: A teenager gasps, freezes or stares at shocking news such as unexpected results. Astonishment is stronger than surprise and can lead to joy or distress, so a moment of quiet space helps.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager before a trip, exam or first job interview may feel eager and anxious at once, with the same racing heart. Labelling it as excitement can turn nervous energy into readiness.

rows.description: A teenager cheers, pumps a fist or hugs teammates after a win. Triumph feels good and is best shared graciously, since gloating can hurt others.

rows.description: A teenager who withdraws, answers in single words or stares at a screen may be tired, hurt, private or bored. Detachment has many causes, so patient check-ins over time are better than accusations.
